# **HIGHER EDUCATION POLICY IN SOUTH AFRICA:** **WHO'S AGENDA?**
# **André Theys**
## **Introduction**
The unbanning of political liberation movements and the release of Nelson Mandela in 1990 started the political change in South Africa that culminated in the 1994 national elections. This led to the replacement of the apartheid government with a Government of National Unity, led by the African National Congress (ANC). Scholars have analysed this period and while they might categorise the periods differently they agree on a number of identifiable phases. While Kraak (2001) noted five such phases, Jansen (2003) describes the period 1990 to 1994 as a *period of policy positioning* and the period from 1994 to 1999 as a *period of policy * *pronouncements*. 1994 to 1997, or the *legislative era* (Kraak 2001), saw significant education legislation enacted by the South African Parliament, culminating in the passing of the Higher Education Act of 1997. The next few years saw some implementation of the policy. However, with the limits of state power realised and the idealism of the Higher Education Act (1997) mediated by structural constraints Kraak saw this as the *era of * *policy doubt and retraction* (Kraak 2004)*. *During this period, with a new Minister of Education appointed, discursive tensions and political difficulties reached a peak but nonetheless the National Plan for Higher Education in South Africa (of 2001) was released.
In his 2002 paper entitled *Political symbolism as policy craft: explaining non-reform in South African education after * *apartheid*, Jansen draws on seven case studies to construct *political symbolism* as going some way to theorising and explaining what he terms as *one of the most intractable problems in policy studies, the distance between policy * *ideals and practical outcomes*? He suggests that while South Africa's education policies as text were impressive, they did not have implementation as their primary commitment; that the making of education policy in South Africa was about achieving a political statement to mark the shift from apartheid to postapartheid, and *was not connected to any serious intention to change practice on the ground* (Jansen 2002),
In trying to understand whether Jansen's assertions have merit I focus on two specific policy documents for analysis, namely the Higher Education Act of 1997 and the National Plan for Higher Education in South Africa of 2001. While there are many other policy documents that impact higher education in South Africa a review of all of them is not possible for this paper. It is my contention that the two aforementioned policy documents have impacted higher education and continue to do so. I will review policy formulation theories and frameworks followed by reviewing only the agenda setting and implementation stages of these policy documents with a focus on only one implementation aspect, namely, that of institutional mergers.
## **Theories of Policy Making**
Policy analysis, with its origins in the 1950s is commonly perceived as a process developing through a sequence of discreet stages or phases. This set of stages, cycle or framework, while critiqued in terms of its theoretical construction, being normative and prescriptive as opposed to being analytical and descriptive has endured serving as a basic template for policy analysis or as a starting point for typologies of the policy
process. Modelling the policy process as stages was first postulated by American political scientist and communications theorist, Harold Dwight Lasswell in 1956 (Jann & Wegrich 2007) and was later refined by other scholars such as Brewer, deLeon, May and Wildavsky (DeLeon & Weible 2010). Laswell's original model, made up of seven stages of intelligence, promotion, prescription, invocation, application, termination and appraisal has since evolved into the more contemporary approach of *agenda-setting*, *policy formulation*, *decision making*, *implementation* and *evaluation* (Jann & Wegrich 2007). DeLeon and Weible (2010) describe these stages best in their commentary on Laswell's vision as the ways citizens struggle to define issues as problems worthy of attention on government agendas, how governments analyse problems, formulate and select from policy alternatives, how governments implement policy, how these policies are evaluated, built on or even terminated. I contend that this is not too dissimilar to Argentine philosopher Mario Bunge's *technological rule* and expanded on by Pawson and Tilley for organisational and management studies (Denyer et al. 2008). Denyer et al (2008) refer to their work as *CIMO-logic* and is based on Bunge's rule, that if you want to achieve outcome *O* in context *C*, then use intervention *I*, with Pawson and Tilley adding the issue of causality, by asking through which mechanism *M*, does the intervention produce an outcome in the given context. Referring this back to the policy cycle, the policy environment is seen as context *C*, the mechanism *M* is the proposed policy, the intervention *I* is the implementation of the policy while the outcome *O* is the intended solutions, evaluation and possible termination.
In reality the policy process rarely if ever follows such a logical sequence with *clear-cut beginnings and * *endings,* with policies constantly under review, manipulated, tweaked, implemented and not implemented. Despite its limitations and critique from noted policy scholars such as Paul Sabatier (DeLeon & Weible 2010), the policy cycle has become the most widely applied framework to systematise and organise research on public policy (Jann & Wegrich 2007), even though rarely applied in its entirety.
## **Agenda Setting**
The first stage of the policy cycle is agenda setting, where problems and possible solutions grab or lose the attention of the citizenry, governments or elite groups. Dramatic policy changes are generally associated with increased government attention to an issue and policies are often developed or amended significantly during relatively short *windows of opportunity*, during which circumstances and conditions were temporarily favourable for this increased attention or action (Baumgartner et al. 2006). An agenda, which can be a series of problems, understandings of causes, symbols or solutions can be as defined as an act before a parliament or as vague as a series of assumptions and beliefs around a possible problem and what ought to be done by governments, the public and or other organisations (Birkland 2007; Karch 2012). Agendas exist in all spheres of government and systematic research first emerged with the critique of pluralism in the United States. Some scholars suggested that political debates result in agenda setting which emerges from the conflict between political actors where a less powerful actor will seek to raise issues onto the agenda by expanding a conflict, while others have suggested the agenda setting arises through a process of filtering of problems and issues resulting in some problems or issues deliberately left off of an agenda (Jann & Wegrich 2007). Other studies reveal that it is not so much the scale of a particular problem that surfaces the problem to the agenda,
but rather the attachment of particular images or symbols of the problem or assumed solution that have been identified as an important variable in agenda setting. Wolf et al (2013) contend that agenda setting in terms of policy process is *fundamentally about the politics of attention and attention dynamics at the level of the political * *system*.
While recognising and defining problems are perceived in liberal democracies as being conducted in the public, media (Wolfe et al. 2013; Eissler et al. 2014) or communities, the actual agenda setting is characterised by different patterns in terms of stakeholder make-up. The generally perceived pattern where social actors force governments to place issues on the agenda by way of public support is but one type of agenda setting. Other significant patterns are where interest groups with direct access to governments, for example consider the lobbyists in the United States, and are capable of placing topics on the agenda without recognition of the public. Despite these differing patterns of agenda setting, liberal democracies and modern societies are typified by the distinctive role of the public and media on agenda setting or policy making, particularly when risks emerge. Often governments are faced with limited options and simply cannot ignore public sentiment without risking credibility or legitimacy.
The coming together of numerous variables and interconnected factors determines whether an issue becomes a major topic on the policy agenda and can include material conditions of the policy environment such as the level of economic development, the ideologies of the actors, flow of ideas and so forth. While earlier models of agenda setting focused on social and economic aspects as variables, Jann and Wegrich (2007) cite the work of Baumgartner and Jones, whose more recent approaches have stressed the role of ideas expressed in public and professional discourses, introducing the notion of policy monopoly as *the monopoly * *of political understandings*. Baumgartner and Jones suggested that agenda setting and policy change happened when *policy monopolies* become increasingly contested and previous actors who were disinterested become mobilised. Agenda setting is certainly not a rational selection of issues in terms of their relevance as a problem of society but rather how the variables such as the actors, institutions, material conditions and ideas interact being highly contingent on a specific set of circumstances and conditions. Jann and Wegrich (2007) deems Kingdon's *multiple streams model* to be most influential as it builds on Cohen, March and Olsen's 1972 *garbage can* model of organisational choice. Kingdon introduced the notion of *windows of * *opportunity* that open up at a specific time for a specific policy. The policy window typically opens with three discreet *streams* intersecting, (i) the policy stream seen as solutions, (ii) the politics stream seen as changes in government or public sentiment and (iii) the problem stream or perception of the problem.
### *Political Power in Agenda Setting*
The ability of citizenry, governments or elite groups to influence policy is not just a function of who makes the most persuasive argument, be it empirical or rhetorical. Some groups are just more powerful than others in that they are better able to influence the outcomes of policy debates. Considering power, citizenry, governments or elite groups (Eissler et al. 2014) can either force others to do things against their will, what Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz referred to as coercive power in their classic *American Political Science * *Review* 1962 article, or to prevent them from doing things they want to do, what they referred to as *blocking *
[FIGURE: see A2.R38_fig01.jpg]
*power* (Birkland 2007). In the former case, groups participating in making decisions that affect others regardless of whether they approve of the decisions or consequences is a classic case of power typically seen in totalitarian or authoritarian regimes, although also possible in liberal democracies as well. In the latter case, groups prevent the interests of others from getting on to the agenda or becoming policy, despite the latter group wanting the interests raised on to the agenda. The idea of power is complex and a highly researched field within political science and is relevant in this case as it helps unpack how groups compete to gain access to the agenda setting and deny other groups' access to the agenda setting.
Birkland references E. E. Schattschneider's theories of group mobilisation and participating in agenda setting which rests on his cited postulation that issues are generally elevated to the agenda when the scope of conflict is broadened. The two ways that maligned groups broaden the scope of conflict is (i) when they go public making use of images and symbols thereby inducing public sympathy and greater media interest, and (ii) when they appeal to higher decision-making bodies. Birkland (2007) showcases the first example by citing the environmental groups who make use of symbols or images showing damage by humans such as the deforestation or the wandering polar bear to bear witness to the melting polar ice. As mentioned previously, successful policy advocacy depends on the ability to tell a good story which requires the use of symbols to advance an argument. Politics is full of symbols, those perceived as good, and others as bad, while others are considered controversial and as such can serve as a source of consensus or differentiation (Cobb & Elder 1972; Wolfe et al. 2013). A symbol can be anything that represents something else and its meaning will depend on people's interpretation, use and response thereof (Cobb & Elder 1972; Birkland 2007).
When powerful groups lose control of the agenda, less powerful groups can enter policy debates to garner the attention of their constituencies. The greater attention to the problem can increase negative public sentiment towards the status quo triggering the agenda changes leading to lasting policy change that break up Baumgartner and Jones' *policy monopolies*. This is also the opening of Kingdon's *window of opportunity* (Birkland 2007). One shortcoming of these power theories is that some groups simply accept their fate and do not challenge the elite groups in control of the agenda setting and associated to this is the notion that elite groups are single-minded and in agreement with regards the issues on the agenda. On the contrary, powerful groupings with similar social and economic interests often conflict with each other around the same issues. Similarly, many groupings that seek to change policy are advocated by people with similar socioeconomic backgrounds (Birkland 2007).
### *Problem Definition and Social Construction*
[FIGURE: see A2.R38_fig02.jpg]
The process of defining a problem (Wolfe et al. 2013) and selling this to the public is called *social construction*. Social construction are the ways in which citizens who make up society and the differing interests contesting within that society, structure and tell the stories about how the problems came to be the way they are. A group able to develop and promote the most effective depiction of an issue has the advantage in contesting what will be done about the problem (Birkland 2007). Whether a problem really is a problem is not sufficient in political and policy debates. Defining the problem is also not sufficient, but rather the ability for
[FIGURE: see A2.R38_fig03.jpg]
one group to persuade others that the problem exists and is real, is necessary. The social construction of a problem is part of the political, ideological and social structures at a particular point in time, and the value system of a society or grouping will determine how different polices will result from constructing problems differently.

It is during this stage of the policy cycle that problems are expressed; proposals and demands are made in concrete government proposals and will include the definition of objectives, in other words, what the policy under consideration should set out to achieve. The consideration of alternatives for action will also be included in this stage. While early studies of this stage placed importance on the government bureaucracy and professional civil servants in policy formulation, these groups are not separated from the citizenry when formulating policies. Later studies from the 1970s and 1980s developed more elaborate theories and the concept of *policy networks* became more prominent. These networks were characterised *by non-hierarchical , * *horizontal relationships between actors inside the network* (Jann & Wegrich 2007). While these interactions between governments and its citizenry are ever present, the particular collection of actors within these policy networks differ from policy domain to policy domain, as well as between countries with differing political and ideological cultures and traditions. These differences give rise to national styles of policy making from a policy instrument point of view.
## **Implementation**
The stage of execution of a policy by the responsible government institutions or organisations, which is not always necessarily within the public sector, is referred to as implementation. Broadly speaking, policy implementation is what occurs between government's intention to do something or stop doing something and it actually happening. This stage is critical as political and administrative actions on the ground are not always rolled out optimally or as intended given the inevitable loss of control accompanying government bureaucracy. Consequently, policies and their intentions are often revised, distorted, delayed or prevented from implementation (Jann & Wegrich 2007). Thus, an ideal implementation stage would include (i) elements of a specification of programme details, (ii) the allocation of resources, and (iii) elements of how decisions will be taken.
Early policy cycle research did not recognise implementation as a discrete stage. What happened after an act was passed by a parliament was not perceived as problematic, the underlying assumption being that once government passed the act, legislation or law, the business of policy making was complete. This changed with the seminal study entitled *How Great Expectations in Washington are dashed in Oakland*, by Pressman and Wildavsky on the implementation of an unemployment programme for members of a minority group in Oakland, California (Jann & Wegrich 2007).
Policy implementation studies, found at the intersection of organisational theory, public management studies and political science have been broadly characterised as studies of policy change and have had three generations of implementation research identified (Pulzl & Treib 2007). The three generations can be
subdivided into three distinct theoretical approaches, (i) top-down models, where the main emphasis is on the decision makers to produce policy objectives and control implementation thereof, (ii) bottom-up models which as a result of a critique of the top-down models view local bureaucrats as the main actors in policy delivery, with implementation negotiated within implementers networks, and (iii) hybrid theories, which attempt to overcome the divide between the top-down and bottoms-up models.
Top-down theories rose from the assumption that policy implementation starts with decisions made by central government, essentially the *black box model* inspired by systems analysis. This assumed a direct causal link between policies and observed outcomes while discounting the implementers' impact on policy delivery (Pulzl & Treib 2007). It was therefore implicit in the implementation that adequate bureaucratic structures and procedures existed or were established to make sure that policies were executed as accurately as possible. Thus, the bureaucratic structures or implementers should have at their disposal adequate resources with a system of clear responsibilities and hierarchical control ensuring supervision of the implementers. American scholars, Van Meter and Van Horn in 1975 offered an evolved theoretical model which accounted for six variables shaping the relationships between policy formulation and outcome. While many of these dealt with organisational capacity and hierarchical control, two variables departed from the mainstream top-down theory which was (i) the extent of policy change and (ii) the degree of consensus. These two were considered important for effective implementation. Other scholars such as Sabatier and Mazmanian, who in 1979 were proponents of the top-down approach, assumed a clear separation between policy formation and policy implementation. Their model also listed six criteria for effective implementation. They were (i) policy objectives needing to be clear and consistent, (ii) the policy programme should have a valid causal theory, (iii) the implementation process must be structured adequately, (iv) bureaucratic structures or implementers must be committed to the programmes goals, (v) interest groups, government and bureaucratic structures must be supportive, and (vi) there should be no detrimental changes to the socioeconomic conditions (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
Bottom-up theories emerged between the late 1970s and early 1980s as a critical reaction to the top-down school with a number of studies observing that political outcomes did not relate sufficiently to the original policy objectives and significantly, the assumed causal theory was questionable. Scholars advised studying the reality of what was actually happening on the ground, at the level of the recipient and analysing what really influenced the action on the ground. These studies typically rejected the centrally defined policies with implementers sticking to the objectives and started from the *bottom*, identifying the network of actors in actual policy delivery. American researchers Lipsky and Elmore as well as Swedish scholar Hjern were classical bottoms-up researchers and joined later by other authors such as Porter and Hull. Lipsky looked at the behaviour of public service workers such as doctors, teachers, police officers and so forth, which he termed *street level bureaucrats*, arguing that policy analysts should consider the interactions between these workers and the citizenry. Hjern, in collaboration with Porter and Hull, developed an empirical network methodology to study the implementation process. They suggested that implementation analysis should identify networks of all actors from all the relevant agencies involved in implementation followed by
observing how they solve problems. Sabatier in 1986 thought this was a useful tool to describe *implementation structures* (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
The two approaches are based on different models of democracy. Top-down theorists' foundations are in the traditional representative democracy model whereby elected representatives are legitimised to bind citizenry to their decisions and ensure that their decisions are carried out accurately. Put another way, any deviation from their policy objectives is perceived as a violation of democratic standards. Bottoms-up theorists differ fundamentally, emphasizing that *street level bureaucrats*, impacted target groups and individual actors have interests that need to be taken into account, and that elites disregarding these interests lead to illegitimate decisions (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
Given the debate between, researchers such as Sabatier, Elmore and Goggin amongst others have tried to reconcile both approaches by combining elements of both schools while avoiding the conceptual weaknesses of both. Moving away from his earlier works with Mazmanian, Sabatier argued in 1986 for his *advocacy * *coalition framework*, which rejected the stages model of the policy cycle explaining policy change as a whole. Winter in 1990 contributed to overcoming the separation of policy formation and implementation while still embracing the stages model. Sabatier and Winter raised awareness through their hybrid approach that one cannot analyse implementation without looking at the policy formulation process (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
## *New Developments *
One new development in implementation analysis is the *interpretative approach*. This approach considers the strict distinction underlying the positivist philosophy of science as untenable and challenges the notion of unbiased and neutral observations. The interpretative approach ignores the factual basis of problems as a point of reference and instead shows that multiple, ambiguous and conflicting meanings and interpretations can exist in parallel. It too rejects the assumption that implementation can be looked at without considering the policy formulation process. The focus of the interpretative approach lies in the interpretation of the meaning distributed by policy actors, implementation agencies and recipients of the policy. Effectively the written content of policies may only reflect goals that are publicly explained while bureaucratic structures or implementers will also need to implement goals which are not explicit but only tacitly communicated in the policy. In more than thirty years of policy implementation research, five points are worth noting (i) both sides of the debate, top-down and bottoms-up agree that implementation is a continuum between central steer and local autonomy, (ii) the bottoms-up theorists have convinced the community that implementation rests on more than political orders from above, (iii) that implementation and policy formulation are highly interdependent, (iv) that implementation processes should not be viewed in isolation, in other words, away from other policy fields or socioeconomic developments, and (v) that different countries or cultures have different implementation styles and that there is much to be learned from the interpretative and constructivist approaches. These argue that policy objectives and implementation cannot always be objectively discerned and that different perspectives shaped by language, culture and symbolic politics affect implementation (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
## **Evaluation**
The evaluation of the policy cycle is where policy outcomes are evaluated and measured against its intended policy objectives, although not always only performed at the final stage of the cycle resulting in termination of a policy. Rather it may lead to policy tweaking, changes to impetus on the implementation if found to be lacking, or terminated if failing to attain its objectives. Evaluation can also occur at any stage of the policy cycle (Weible et al. 2012).
The purpose of evaluation studies in the policy cycle process is intended to move beyond scientific evaluation studies and should take place at regular intervals, being embedded as part of the political process and debate. Thus scientific evaluation has been distinguished from administrative evaluations conducted by public administrations carried out by diverse actors including the wider public and media. Governance structures that exist in liberal democracies, viz. courts of law, audit offices and think tanks are all considered as part of the evaluation. While evaluation research attempts to establish evaluation as rational evidence based policy making, it is regularly exposed to specific logic and incentives of the political process. In one way the assessment of policy outputs and outcomes are biased according to the interests and values of particular actors, particularly where the shifting of blame for poor performance has become integral to politics.
Evaluations may lead to different patterns of policy learning in terms of feedback mechanisms or a potential resetting of the policy cycle. One pattern could be that successful policies are reinforced or that failed policies are terminated, which scholars agree seems rather difficult to enforce in real world conditions given the patterns of modern day policy formulation, for example budget cuts, removal of state subsidies and so forth, all leading to unintended consequences (Jann & Wegrich 2007).
## **Higher Education Policy in South Africa**
Having reviewed policy cycle theory I now shift focus to higher education policy in South Africa looking at its origins and then moving into the two policy documents. During the mid-1800s white South Africans obtained access to higher education by earning degrees from the University of London. While the colonial government established the University of the Cape of Good Hope, modelled on the University of London, in 1873 and Scottish missionaries established the forerunner to the University of Fort Hare in 1915, the formalising of higher education only occurred in 1916. It was in 1916 that the government of the day passed the Higher Education Act bringing all university colleges under the control of a Minister of Education.
The University of the Cape of Good Hope became the University of South Africa with all the colleges affiliated until such time that they met the criteria for full university status.
This marked the period when the South African College would become the University of Cape Town, the Victoria College would become the University of Stellenbosch, the South African School of Mines and Technology would become the University of the Witwatersrand and the Transvaal University College, the University of Pretoria (Mouton et al. 2013).
By 1974 the Van Wyk De Vries Commission of Inquiry into higher education was completing its work (Mouton et al. 2013) and proposed a *trinary* model which maintained that universities should concentrate on teaching and research of the basic fundamental principles of science, that technikons (a South African equivalent of the international polytechnic) should concentrate on the application of scientific principles to practical problems, and that technical colleges (since renamed Further Education and Training or FET colleges) should provide technical and vocational education and training (Kraak 2004). This rigid differentiation remained in place until the 1990s when South African politics started to normalise with the unbanning of the political liberation movements and critical debates around higher education were initiated.
After convening South Africa's first non-racial elections in 1994, the ANC-led government was under pressure to demonstrate how it would serve the aspirations of the black population who had struggled for decades against colonialism and apartheid. Thus, the newly formed government raced to establish education policy for the nascent democracy (Jansen 2001). Kraak (2004) notes that in the case of higher education, there was no consensus amongst the higher education community with regard to the content of a new policy framework, and that there existed *a high degree of discursive tensions and competing interpretations* that came to characterise the policy formulation during that period, that which led up to and culminated in the adoption of the Higher Education Act of 1997 and the National Plan for Higher Education in South Africa of 2001.
The making of modern South African education policy is described as *a struggle for the achievement of a broad * *political symbolism that would mark the shift from apartheid to a post-apartheid society* (Jansen 2002). Kraak (2004) contends that there were several competing discourses impacting on higher education policy formulation in South Africa between 1990 and 2002. In particular, the importing of international policy into South Africa clashed with the local educational discourse that had evolved historically on both sides of the political centre. Kraak (2001) identified five overlapping phases during the period where education policy was being formulated. The first, what Kraak terms *the pre-**"taking of power" phase* commenced around 1989 where the liberation movements moved from struggle politics to a mode whereby they were *preparing to govern*. The second phase, or *legislative era*, happened between 1994 and 1997 where education legislation was enacted by Parliament, with the adoption of the Higher Education Act of 1997. The third phase or *policy implementation * *phase* overlapped the second phase and was the time when the government started grappling with the limits of its power; its idealism having been mediated by the structural constraints it faced then. Kraak refers to the fourth phase as *a vacillating state, the era of policy doubt and retraction* and identifies it where the *complexities * *of governance in the new state start to emerge*. It was during this phase, around 1999 to 2000 that the discourse and political tensions reached a crescendo which resulted in substantial policy uncertainty, withdrawal and reversal. The fifth and final phase was characterised by the release of the National Plan in February of 2001. It was the release of this policy documentation that saw the government confirm its support for the Higher Education Act's key policy principles and adopt a new resolve to implement them (Kraak 2001).
This paper examines the agenda setting of both policy documents through the use of *CIMO-logic* (Denyer et al. 2008) and limits its focus to reviewing only what led up to the formulation of the policies, which is the
context *C*, during that period. The intervention *I* already exists, that being the two policy documents under review, the mechanism *M* being the actual policy implementation, that which we are currently experiencing and the outcome *O*, being the policy objectives, which time will still reveal. Examining only the agenda setting phase or context is not out of step with typical policy cycle research approaches and this paper's approach is informed by Kingdon's *multiple streams theory* (Jann & Wegrich 2007).
### **National Commission of Higher Education**
The ANC-led government inherited a higher education system which was shaped by political, social and economic inequalities of race, class and gender bestowed by the history of apartheid (Shrivastava & Shrivastava 2014). In terms of the policy cycle, and while there were discursive tensions (Kraak 2004), the problem definition appeared clear and there was agreement that any higher education policy had to emphasize higher education not only as human resource development but also as being vital to social and economic transformation (Nieuwenhuis 1997; Rensburg 2001; Shrivastava & Shrivastava 2014). Despite this agreement towards the overall goal, the tensions within the higher education community remained and there were competing interpretations. The drawing on of international policy clashed with the South African educational discourses that had evolved on both sides of the political centre. Jansen (2002) noted that there were few countries in post-colonial Africa that had drawn more heavily on international experts and consultants as South Africa had done during this period, especially used up to and during the National Commission of Higher Education (NCHE) during the 1990s.
Prior to the NCHE, sector assessments such as the *Primary Education Sector Assessments* and *Tertiary Education * *Sector Assessments* were undertaken, driven largely by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) which commissioned consultancy teams consisting of South Africans but predominantly American experts, with a view to recommending policy for the incoming ANC-led government. Locally, the ANC-aligned policy organisations such as the Centre for Educational Policy Development (CEPD) and the Education Policy Units (EPUs) conducted their own education policy research. It was the EPUs that would go on to propel the National Education Policy Investigation (NEPI), which in 1992 was mandated to *develop policy options for the democratic movement* (Jansen 2003). It is not clear to what extent the sector assessments impacted education policy between 1992 and 1996 and while the NEPI published some twelve reports covering curriculum and post-secondary education which were expanded by the CEPD into more detailed planning documents, the NEPI research was understandably conducted without knowing how the political transition would unfold. Essentially, while the NEPI provided a *values * *framework* for policy formulation, it did not provide real content for the ANC-led government higher education policy, post 1994 (Jansen 2003). Following NEPI, Kraak (2004) deemed the NCHE to be the most influential policy formulation exercise in higher education. The NCHE proposed a new higher education policy framework in 1996 predicated on five key pillars (i) a single nationally coordinated system, (ii) increased access and raised participation rates, (iii) increased responsiveness to societal and economic needs, (iv) programme differentiation with the development of institutional niche areas, and (v) a planning and coordination imperative.
### **The Higher Education Act of 1997**
The NCHE framework was largely accepted by the government in the passing of the Higher Education Act of 1997. The Act regulated higher education, provided for the establishment of a Council on Higher Education (CHE), provided for the establishment, governance and funding of public higher education institutions, provided for the appointment of an independent assessor, the registration of private higher education institutions, quality assurance and promotion in higher education, provided for the transitional arrangements and repealed the previous laws pertaining to higher education (Higher Education Act No 101 1997). Despite this, much of the new policy regime had not been implemented by 2001, reinterpreted or revised, which Kraak (2001, 2004) contends was due to heightened discursive tensions around competing ideas on how higher education had to transformed, what he termed as policy mediation.
### *Policy Mediation*
Globalisation had brought with it the *high skills thesis* (Ashton 2005), which sees educational reform as one part of a larger set of socioeconomic reforms leading to a more highly skilled workforce and ultimately better competitiveness for a country. The high skills thesis played a large role in ANC macro-economic policy from 1990 to 1994, linking educational reform with macro-economic and labour restructuring and was factored in the ANC's first macro-economic policy framework, termed *Growth through Redistribution*, defined in collaboration with economists aligned to the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) (Kraak 2001; 2004). This framework was the precursor to the ANC's *Reconstruction and Development Programme* (RDP). The RDP comprising four pillars, that of meeting basic needs, developing human resources, building the economy and democratising the state consciously, sought to link economic policy with other policy domains, notably, employment and labour market reform, education and training, public works and so forth. This was effectively, *joined-up policy* (Kraak et al. 2006) espoused in the high skills thesis. The RDP showed understanding that neither a commandist central planning system nor a laissez faire free market approach would solve South Africa's problems and advocated for an *enabling state that was slim but * *intervening strategically* when required to do so. This was evidence of the reconciliatory and consensual politics necessary at the time but overshadowed the left-right, socialist-capitalist tensions.
Another significant tension was the consolidation of radical-progressive propositions on education reform with its roots in the People's Education movement of the 1980's. People's Education was a political movement that saw the classroom as a central site of opposition to apartheid representing a pedagogical alternative to the one imposed by the apartheid state, but by the 1990s had grown to be the oppositional discourse on the concept of equity (Kraak 2001; Kraak 2004). Their concept of equity called for social and institutional transformation to remove the inequalities of the previous regime and this appealed to the majority of staff and students of the previously disadvantaged, largely black, institutions. They argued for these institutions to be brought on par with the previously advantaged, largely white, institutions. The demands for economic development and the demands for equity were viewed by some education policy analysts as contradictory to each other. Analysts like Badat, Barron, Fisher, Pillay and Wolpe argued that international experience had shown favouring one goal would threaten the other. With this *equity versus *
*development* tension remaining throughout 1990 to 1997, although largely displaced with expert-led multistakeholder policy processes privileging other discourses, the new state remained cautious not to privilege one over the other (Kraak 2004).
A further discursive tension was what Kraak (2004) termed *stratification thinking*. This is a discourse that had its roots in the policies of the apartheid government, notably the 1974 adoption of the trinary model proposed by the Van Wyk De Vries Commission of Inquiry (1973). By 2004, this fairly rigid differentiation of function between institutions was still largely prevalent, despite the former Department of National Education acknowledging in 1995 its dissatisfaction with its rigidity, inflexibility and isolationist functioning. The NCHE viewed its solution for a single coordinated system as the compromise in a heated and contested space. Despite the NCHE's proposal of *a continuum along which the system could move over time * *from functional differentiation towards a single system with softened boundaries*, dissenting voices remained. In a 1996 minority report, the vice chancellor of the then called Peninsula Technikon, opposed the notion of differentiation being based on programme rather than institutions. His view was that it would negate the current institutional missions and cultures and he predicted academic creep with vocational education and training being side-lined in favour of perceived higher status academic programmes (Kraak 2004; Figaji 2016).
### *Structural Limits*
Kraak (2001; 2004) maintains that all these aforementioned discursive tensions resulted in there being no *strong binding consensus* across the higher education communities in support of the official policy enacted by the new government. In addition to this, there were other factors such as the new state's lack of capacity (Rensburg 2001; Jansen 2003) preventing the use of envisaged planning and coordination levers. There were also further structural limits to implementation such as fiscal restraint and a shifting macro-economic policy when in 1996 the ANC released the Growth, Employment and Redistribution (GEAR) strategy. GEAR displaced the RDP, the ANC's social democratic orthodoxy with a more conservative macro-economic strategy seeking to reduce the state's fiscal deficit and inflation rate and this effectively neutralised COSATU and the Communist Party as stakeholders in the agenda setting of policy formulation. The impact of GEAR on higher education was also severe as government stabilised education expenditure (Shrivastava & Shrivastava 2014), not only decreasing the *real* funding between 1995 to 1999, but also signalling that any higher education transformation would need to be met through institutional efficiencies, cost effectiveness and a redistribution of these savings. In the absence of any fiscal capacity, the state had no alternative but to *play up the symbolic value of the policies* having been undermined by the economic choices of GEAR (Jansen 2002). While scholars such as Kraak and Rensburg noted GEAR's neoliberal conservatism as limiting funding required for the new policies, it should be noted that Jansen argues that while he is not claiming that financial constraints are irrelevant he is arguing that it is precisely because of the constraints that the state is having to *play up the symbolic value of the policies*. Ironically Jansen notes that had there been no constraints, it does not necessarily hold true that policy would have been implemented.
Jansen (2002) also noted *the symbolic value of policy gaining capital* with the citizenry due to the limiting factor the South African Constitution had on policy implementation. As a consequence of the constitutional limitations, education policy implementation was a provincial competency (Rensburg 2001) meaning that central government was largely impotent in driving implementation as it would be contravening the constitution. By taking a conservative interpretation of the constitution the then Ministry of Education had actually weakened its own authority in terms of provincial regulation.
### **The National Plan for Higher Education of 2001**
The final phase in the development of higher education policy began in February of 2001 with the release of the National Plan for Higher Education (NPHE). The NPHE, organised in six sections across eighty-six pages, announced sixteen outcomes described as *system wide targets* and *goals*. The outcomes were to be achieved through *levers* or *steering mechanisms* (Department of Education 2001). While Kraak (2001) maintains that the NPHE's main purpose was to reaffirm the principles of the Act of 1997, Jansen (2001) questions whether the NPHE could deliver on the transformation imperatives, whether it addressed the critical issues facing institutions and if the planned outcomes could be achieved with the strategies suggested.
The NPHE reaffirmed three policy goals, (i) increasing participation rates from 15 percent to 20 percent over the next ten to fifteen years, (ii) the setting of staff and student equity targets for institutions, and (iii) its commitment to a diverse but single coordinated national system. While the NPHE rejected the CHE's rigid structural differentiation it proposed the retention of the binary divide between technikons and universities till 2006, to limit institutional creep and it formulated a plan for the process of institutional restructuring and mergers. The NPHE was seen as the final stage in the on-going policy cycle and while it reaffirmed the policy fundamentals acquired through widespread stakeholder support in the 1990s, it strongly asserted that it (*was)* *not open to further consultation* (Department of Education 2001).
#### *Institutional Mergers *
One of the outcomes of the NPHE was the new institutional and organisational forms using the mechanism of mergers. Jansen (2001) was of the view that the merging of two or more institutions into one single institution was risky regardless of the policy intention, be it combinations, incorporations or mergers. The proposed mergers listed in the NPHE at the time of its release were either already in motion, planned for a number of years prior to the NPHE or were of such that it had none of the historical, political or emotional sensitivities that would have led to confrontation with government. Jansen (2001) noted that institutions to be investigated further by a National Working Group was more likely to be staffed by politicians and trade unionists rather than higher education experts, so as to obtain buy in towards unpopular political decisions.
The institutional mergers that followed were not universally accepted, one example being the merger of the Peninsula Technikon with the Cape Technikon to become the Cape Peninsula University of Technology. The vice chancellor spoke out against his merger, disagreeing with it fundamentally and viewed it as *forced and * *politically motivated* (Figaji 2016).
### **Political Dynamics in South African Higher Education Policy**
Figaji (2016) posited that that the merger decisions were made for political reasons and not for the benefit of the higher education sector. For the policy changes needed by the then Minister of Education, Professor Kader Asmal, he was required by law to consult with the CHE. The Minister then asked the CHE for advice and the CHE convened a committee of which the Professor Figaji was a member. The resulting advice however was not accepted and when the inevitable revolt came from the affected institutions, the Minister advised that he was not going to accept the advice and set up his own committee. This committee, that proposed the institutional mergers to address the institutional instability, advised that the Western Cape institutions be left alone as they were relatively successful. However the Minister advised that he could not be perceived to be leaving the Western Cape alone and merging everywhere else (the Western Cape at this stage was perceived as affiliated to the ANC opposition) and so *had to do something* in the Western Cape (Figaji 2016). After announcing that the Peninsula Technikon and the University of the Western Cape (which shares a common geographical boundary) was to be merged, Figaji wrote a newspaper article sarcastically congratulating the Minister on merging two black institutions while leaving the former white institutions unaffected. The Minister, realising his mistake, withdrew his original plan and merged Peninsula Technikon with the Cape Technikon instead. Figaji (2016) viewed the mergers as a disaster believing that South Africa did not get the diversity of access and opportunities that was originally intended.
Having adopted a bottoms-up approach the state had now moved to a top-down approach to implement, possibly as a way to overcome policy drift. Jansen (2002) cites from the unpublished work of Lodge (undated) entitled *Policy Processes within the ANC and the Tripartite Alliance* which concluded that policy making within the Tripartite Alliance (ANC, Communist Party and COSATU) was participatory and democratic in character up to the 1994 election. Jansen agrees with Lodge that in every single process related to policy formulation throughout the 1990s, there was *an exceptional preoccupation with inclusivity and * *representivity in the make-up of the working groups* (Jansen 2002). However, Jansen's 2000 and 2002 research in attempting to answer why, despite so much education policy formulation after apartheid, there was still so little change in education practice throughout South Africa, found (i) that while groups might be invited to participate, there is no guarantee that their views will prevail, (ii) even though participation in initial debate might be broad policies finally adopted are not discussed or critiqued to same extent, (iii) participating groups have unequal power and expertise in different policy formulation groupings, resulting in differing emphasis in outcomes, (iv) participation only emerges at a point where a policy framework may have already been decided, and (v) participation is confused with consultation, where consultation is simply a matter of securing approval.
Jansen (2002) concluded that the South African post-apartheid government's inability to implement change in educational practice *added to a policy regime reliant on symbolic representations of what could be achieved*. He found little evidence that the ANC moving into government was able to change the rhetorical and radical position of policy into the kinds of technical and political skills required for changing the complex educational landscape inherited from apartheid, positing that *the reliance on symbols* may have worked for
liberation movements, but did not translate into effective policy formulation when these same movements transition into government faced with local and international constraints.
## **Conclusion**
The limitations and critique of the policy cycle gives rise to many other theories and frameworks such as Schneider and Ingram's *Social Construction Framework*, Baumgartner and Jones' *Punctuated Equilibrium * *Theory*, Ostrom's *Institutional Analysis and Development Framework *or Sabatier and Jenkins-Smith's *Advocacy * *Coalition Framework* (DeLeon & Weible 2010; Weible et al. 2012). Notably, they all encompass the study of political behaviour among coalitions, groups and citizens, the role of experts and citizens, social constructions, power and inequalities (DeLeon & Weible 2010), hence this paper's analysis informed by the policy cycle, Kingdon's *Multiple Streams Theory* and Denyer et al's *CIMO-logic*.
Reviewing the agenda setting of the two policy documents, the context *C* and the mergers, the mechanism, *M* in terms of *CIMO-logic* it is evident that as the ANC-led government came to power it adopted a bottomsup approach, effectively what had been its culture when still a liberation movement. However, as it transitioned to government, coming to grips with power and its capacity to govern, it adopted a more topdown approach to implement its policies. This would not be an unusual approach for any country whether developmental or the first world, except for Jansen's assertions.
While Jansen lies the blame for what he perceives as lack of implementation at the feet of government, his interpretation of implementation differs from government and any lack of implementation is not squarely on government's shoulders. In terms of Sabatier and Mazmanian's 1979 criteria for effective implementation (Pulzl & Treib 2007), South Africa's case only satisfied half the criteria. There was evidence of limited commitment and support from the bureaucratic structures and implementers (Rensburg 2001) and the adoption of macroeconomic policies had seismic effects on resource allocation to higher education (Nieuwenhuis 1997; Kraak 2001; 2004; Jansen 2003; Shrivastava & Shrivastava 2014). In terms of Kingdons' theory, the policy and problem stream clearly intersected with the political stream but the political dynamics at the time advantaged the political stream over that of the policy and problem streams. It is claimed that what advocates of the hybrid theory overlook is the different perspectives policy formulation stakeholders hold in the allocation of power over the determination of the policy outcomes in terms of democratic theory. There has been increased awareness among scholars that policy implementation is a political process and implementation is often obstructed by the political resistance of the policy formulation stakeholders (Pulzl & Treib 2007).
Besides a critical analysis of higher education in South Africa this paper also attempted to ascertain whether Jansen's assertions were merited. I conclude that while it is evident that much of South Africa's higher education policy formulation made use of political symbolism, I found little evidence that it was never their intention to implement effectively. After all, Weible et al (2012) concluded after much study, that there were *no guarantees for influencing the policy process*.
